Salt was taxed and Indians could not make it. Across India tens of thousands were jailed for making or selling salt, and the march drew the world's attention to the freedom struggle.

entries.name: Charles Darwin
entries.summary: An English naturalist who sailed round the world on HMS Beagle from 1831 to 1836, studying fossils, earthquakes, coral reefs and the animals of the Galápagos. At Down House in Kent he worked out evolution by natural selection, reached independently by Alfred Russel Wallace, and set it out in On the Origin of Species in 1859.

entries.name: The voyage of the Beagle
entries.summary: HMS Beagle left Plymouth in December 1831 to survey the coasts of South America, with the young Charles Darwin aboard as naturalist. In almost five years it went round the world, by Brazil, Patagonia, Tierra del Fuego, Chile, the Galápagos, Australia and the Cape. Darwin's notes, fossils and specimens from the voyage seeded his theory of evolution.

entries.name: On the Origin of Species
entries.summary: Charles Darwin's book, published in London on 24 November 1859, argued that species change over generations by natural selection: individuals with helpful variations survive and breed more. It gathered evidence from breeding, fossils, geography and anatomy. Alfred Russel Wallace had reached the same idea. Backed since by genetics, it is the foundation of modern biology.

entries.name: The hunt for the elements
entries.summary: For most of history people knew a handful of elements, such as gold, iron and sulphur. From Brand’s phosphorus in 1669, chemists isolated dozens more with fire, electricity and the spectroscope. Mendeleev’s periodic table of 1869 predicted the missing ones, and from 1937 physicists made new ones, until in 2016 the seventh row of 118 was full.

entries.name: The periodic table
entries.summary: In 1869 Dmitri Mendeleev in St Petersburg arranged the known elements by atomic weight into columns of elements that behave alike, leaving gaps for undiscovered ones. Lothar Meyer drew a similar table. Gallium (1875), scandium (1879) and germanium (1886) filled three of the gaps with properties Mendeleev had predicted, and the table became the map of chemistry.

entries.name: The noble gases
entries.summary: In 1894 Lord Rayleigh and William Ramsay found argon in air, a gas that reacted with nothing. Ramsay found helium on Earth in 1895 and, with Morris Travers, neon, krypton and xenon in 1898: a whole column the periodic table had lacked. Rayleigh won the 1904 Nobel Prize in Physics and Ramsay the prize in Chemistry.

entries.name: Technetium, the first made element
entries.summary: In 1937 Emilio Segrè and Carlo Perrier in Palermo found element 43 in a strip of molybdenum bombarded in Ernest Lawrence’s cyclotron at Berkeley. It filled one of the gaps Moseley had found, and was the first element made by people rather than found. Named technetium, ‘artificial’, it is now used in tens of millions of medical scans a year.

entries.name: The journey of zero
entries.summary: Babylonian scribes marked an empty place in numbers, and the Maya invented a zero of their own. In India a dot marked the empty place in decimal numbers, and in 628 CE Brahmagupta gave rules for calculating with zero as a number. Through Baghdad and al-Khwarizmi the Indian numerals reached North Africa, then Europe with Fibonacci’s Liber Abaci in 1202.

entries.name: Brahmagupta
entries.note: He gives his own birth year as 598; the year of his death is not known, and 668 is an estimate.
entries.summary: An astronomer and mathematician of Bhillamala, in what is now Rajasthan. In 628 CE he wrote the Brahmasphutasiddhanta, a verse work on astronomy that gave the first known rules for calculating with zero and with negative numbers, which he called debts. Translated into Arabic in Baghdad, his work helped carry Indian numerals and methods west.

entries.name: al-Khwarizmi
entries.note: His dates are known only roughly.
entries.summary: A Persian scholar at the House of Wisdom in Baghdad under the caliph al-Ma’mun. His book al-jabr gave algebra its name, and his book on calculating with Indian numerals, read in Latin as Algoritmi de numero Indorum, spread the decimal numerals and zero to Europe and gave us the word algorithm. He also wrote on astronomy and geography.

entries.name: Fibonacci
entries.note: His dates are known only roughly.
entries.summary: Leonardo of Pisa learned the Indian numerals as a boy in Bugia, in North Africa, where his father served Pisan merchants. His Liber Abaci of 1202 taught Europe’s merchants to calculate with nine figures and zero, and its puzzle about breeding rabbits gave the Fibonacci sequence. The nickname Fibonacci, ‘son of Bonacci’, was given centuries after him.

entries.name: The Sun at the centre
entries.summary: Aristarchus of Samos first proposed that the Earth goes round the Sun, but Ptolemy’s Earth-centred model ruled for 1,400 years. Aryabhata said the Earth spins, and astronomers at Maragha mended Ptolemy’s model. In 1543 Copernicus put the Sun at the centre; Kepler found that orbits are ellipses, Galileo’s telescope found new evidence and Newton’s gravity explained it.

entries.name: Aryabhata
entries.note: His birth year comes from his own statement; the year of his death is not known.
entries.summary: A mathematician and astronomer who wrote the Aryabhatiya in 499 CE, at 23, in 121 Sanskrit verses. He said the Earth spins on its axis, explained eclipses by shadows, gave pi as about 3.1416 and drew up a table of sines. His work was studied across India for a thousand years, and India’s first satellite was named after him.

entries.name: Copernicus
entries.summary: A church canon of Warmia, in what is now Poland, who studied in Kraków and Italy. His On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres, printed in 1543 as he died, put the Sun near the centre with the Earth as a planet spinning daily and circling yearly. It was slow to be accepted, but it began the Scientific Revolution.

entries.name: Kepler
entries.summary: A German mathematician who used Tycho Brahe’s measurements in Prague to show that planets move in ellipses with the Sun at one focus, sweeping equal areas in equal times. His third law, of 1619, linked each planet’s year to its distance from the Sun. He also founded modern optics and produced the most accurate planetary tables of his age.

entries.name: Galileo
entries.summary: A Pisan physicist and astronomer who studied motion by experiment and was among the first to turn a telescope on the sky. In 1610 he found Jupiter’s moons, and he saw the phases of Venus, evidence against the Earth-centred model. Tried by the Inquisition in 1633 for teaching that the Earth moves, he spent his last years under house arrest.

entries.name: Newton
entries.note: Born on 25 December 1642 by the Julian calendar then used in England, 4 January 1643 by the Gregorian.
entries.summary: An English mathematician and physicist whose Principia of 1687 set out the laws of motion and universal gravitation, explaining Kepler’s laws, the tides and the paths of comets with one theory. He also developed calculus, showed that white light is a mix of colours and built the first practical reflecting telescope. He later ran the Royal Mint.

entries.name: The Gene
entries.note: Dated to Mendel's 1866 paper; the story runs to 2025.
entries.summary: From a monk's pea plants to editing the code of life: the story of the gene follows Mendel, Miescher, Avery, Franklin, Watson and Crick, Nirenberg, Sanger, Wilmut, Pääbo, Doudna and Charpentier. It ends with fact and fiction on bringing extinct animals back, from Jurassic Park's amber to today's gene-edited proxies.

entries.name: The structure of DNA
entries.summary: In April 1953 James Watson and Francis Crick published a model of DNA as two strands wound into a helix, with bases pairing A with T and G with C. It rested on Rosalind Franklin's X-ray photograph and Erwin Chargaff's rules, and showed at once how DNA could be copied.

entries.name: Dolly the sheep
entries.summary: Born in July 1996 at the Roslin Institute near Edinburgh, Dolly was the first mammal cloned from an adult cell, her nucleus taken from a ewe's udder. She came from 277 attempts, lived to age six and was announced in 1997. Her birth showed that a grown cell's DNA can be reset.

entries.name: CRISPR gene editing
entries.summary: In 2012 Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier showed that a bacterial immune system, CRISPR-Cas9, could be programmed to cut DNA at a chosen spot. It made gene editing cheap and fast. They won the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry; the first CRISPR medicine, for sickle-cell disease, was approved in 2023.
